ABOUT THIS REPORT
Our reporting scope and boundary
Our Integrated Report covers the Financial Year from 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2023. This report is issued by the Equity 
Group Holdings Plc, which is defined as Equity or the Group. In this report, we update our stakeholders on our financial and 
non-financial performance over the reporting period. The report details our strategy and how we executed through our twin-
engine business model to generate value for our stakeholders.  It further unpacks matters relating to our operating context, 
strategy and business model, performance, governance, and risk management.
We adhere to the principle of integrated thinking in our business operations and reporting. This principle enables us to create 
sustainable value in a collaborative manner while upholding the highest standards of governance aligned to international best 
practice. Our fundamental purpose, is transforming lives, giving dignity, and expanding opportunities for wealth creation.  
This report therefore demonstrates the ways in which we create and deliver value in the short, medium and long-term, which 
we define as one year, two years, five years and beyond, respectively.
Materiality
We consider a material matter to be any issue that has the capacity to impact on the Group’s ability to create sustainable value 
in the short, medium and long term. Through both research and analysis, and our engagement with stakeholders, we strive 
to identify the aspects that present significant risks to our business. We also evaluate how these aspects create opportunities 
to generate and deliver value for our stakeholders. Our process of determining material matters is thus central in guiding our 
decision-making.
Key concepts
Defining value
Value creation is the consequence of how we apply and leverage the capitals available to our business 
to deliver financial and non-financial performance (outputs) and value (outcomes and impacts) for 
stakeholders while making trade-offs. Our value creation process is embedded in our purpose and 
is described as part of our business model and integrated into the way we think, make and process 
decisions.
Materiality and material matters
We apply the principle of materiality in assessing which information is to be included in our Integrated 
Report. This report focuses particularly on those issues, opportunities and challenges that impact 
materially on the Group and its ability to be a sustainable business that consistently delivers stakeholder 
value. Our material matters influence the Group’s strategy and inform the content of this report.
The capitals
Our relevance as a Group today and in the future, and our ability to create long-term value is interrelated 
and fundamentally dependent on the forms of capitals available to us (inputs), how we use these capitals 
(value-adding activities), our impact on them and the value we deliver (outputs and outcomes). We 
consider six essential capitals in line with the International Integrated Reporting Council’s Framework, 
namely financial, manufactured, human, social, cultural and relationship, intellectual, and natural 
capital.

ABOUT THIS REPORT
Our approach to the preparation of our 
Integrated Report
We apply the principle of integrated thinking in preparing 
our Integrated Report. This requires a collaborative process 
across the Group to prepare the content that is presented 
in the report. Information provided in the report is drawn 
from several sources including Board papers and minutes, 
various internal and external reports, stakeholder interviews 
and internally generated management data. Responsible 
members of our management team frame and guide the 
process by making proposals to the report structure and 
concepts and providing information and drafts. The report 
produced is systematically reviewed.  Overall oversight for 
this process is provided by the Executive Management and 
the Board of Directors.
Our reporting frameworks
Our integrated reporting is guided by the principles and 
requirements of the International Integrated Reporting 
Framework <IR>, International Financial Reporting Standard 
(IFRS) and the Code of Corporate Governance for Issuers of 
Securities in Kenya.
As a Kenyan-domiciled Group, we are a licensee of the 
Central Bank of Kenya (CBK), and are listed on the Nairobi 
Securities Exchange (NSE) and cross listed on the Uganda 
Securities Exchange (USE) and the Rwanda Stock Exchange 
(RSE). As such, in drawing up this Integrated Report, we are 
also guided by, and comply with:
• The Banking Act and all prudential guidelines and 
directions given by the CBK and other regional regulators,
• The Companies Act of 2015, (the “Act”) its regulations 
and amendments,
• The Capital Markets Act and all subsidiary legislation,
• The NSE’s rules and guidelines issued by the capital 
markets authorities and securities exchanges in the 
three markets where the Group is listed, together with 
any requirements, decisions, or directions given by these 
authorities and the exchanges,
• The Insurance Act, and its supporting regulations,
• The Retirement Benefits Act, as well as its supporting 
regulations, and
• All other applicable laws and regulations governing the 
various lines of businesses in which we are engaged.
Forward-looking statements
This report contains certain forward-looking statements 
in respect of the Group strategy, performance, and 
operations as well as other geopolitical or macro-economic 
conditions. These forward-looking statements involve 
risk and uncertainty as they relate to future events and 
circumstances which are difficult to predict. They are thus, 
by definition, beyond the Group’s control, and could cause 
our actual results, performance, or achievements to be 
materially different from any future results, performance or 
achievements expressed or implied by such forward-looking 
statements.
Assurance
The Board of Directors ensures the integrity of the 
Integrated Report through adherence to our integrated 
reporting process, with various approvals and signoffs 
undertaken prior to publications by both the Management 
team and the Board.  This process is overseen by the Board 
Audit Committee through deployment of our Enterprise 
Risk Management Framework (ERMF) and internal audit 
procedures. Our annual financial statements as presented 
in this report are assured by our external auditors.

DIRECTORS’ STATEMENT OF RESPONSIBILITY
 
        
___________________
Prof. Isaac Macharia
Chairman
Equity Group Holdings Plc
Our directors have a statutory duty to promote the success of the Group for the benefit of its stakeholders. In promoting 
the success of the Group, directors must have due regard for the long-term consequences of their decisions, the legitimate 
interests of employees, the need to foster effective business relationships with suppliers, customers and others, the impact 
of our operations on the community and the environment, and our desire to maintain our reputation for high standards of 
business conduct.
The Board is committed to ensuring that the Group complies with all laws, regulations and standards applicable to it. The 
Board ensures high standards and practices in corporate governance, and more specifically, that the principles, practices 
and recommendations set out under the Code of Corporate Governance for Issuers of Securities in Kenya (the “Code”) as well 
as the Companies Act of 2015, (the “Act”), are adhered to. The Board has established internal procedures and monitoring 
systems to promote compliance with applicable laws, regulations and standards. The Board is also supported by duly qualified 
legal and compliance professionals to guide and focus the Group’s compliance efforts.
The Board has overall responsibility for good corporate governance across the Group and ensures that its governance policies 
and mechanisms are appropriate to its structure, business and risks. The Board has ensured that there exists comprehensive 
governance documents and regular review and development of new and suitable ones that define the appropriate corporate 
governance principles that will provide fitting incentives for the Group to pursue objectives that are in its best interests, as 
well as those of its shareholders and other stakeholders, whilst protecting their interests. The Board further believes that 
this report fairly represents the Group’s material matters and that it offers a balanced view of the Group’s strategy, business 
model and their implementation.

Overview of Equity Group
Equity Group Holdings Plc is a non-operating holding company offering integrated financial services through banking, 
insurance, technology and philanthropy with subsidiaries in Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, South Sudan and Democratic 
Republic of Congo, a Commercial Representative Office in Ethiopia. The Group operates non-banking subsidiaries in Kenya 
that are engaged in providing investment banking, insurance, custodial, payment and telecommunication services. Equity 
Group Holdings Plc is listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange and cross listed in the Uganda Securities Exchange and the 
Rwanda Stock Exchange.

Our twin engine business model and value creation 
Our twin-engine model comprises of a commercial arm and social impact arm integrating our business approach to the 
market. This approach streamlines operational excellence and fosters collaboration among all our stakeholders. Although 
each operate as separate legal entities, both commercial and social imperatives are integral to our purpose and the objectives 
we purpose to achieve. We view this as a singular approach that is interrelated and synergistic, working collaboratively to 
create shared value for stakeholders. 
Our commercial engine is focused on five distinct elements: Our social engine is focused on seven distinct elements:

•	 Borrow (Lending)
•	 Save (Deposits)
•	 Invest (Wealth Management and Creation)
•	 Insure (Life, Health and Wealth Protection)
•	 Education and Leadership Development
•	 Energy, environment, and climate change 
•	 Enterprise development and financial inclusion
•	 Food and agriculture
•	 Health
•	 Social Protection
•	 Innovation and Technology

and tackle the global crisis of youth unemployment.

Operating context
The post pandemic global order can be typified by two words, volatility and uncertainty. While concerns on inflationary 
pressures and monetary tightening eased at the close of 2023, resolution on heightened interest rates, escalating cost-of-
living, the Russia-Ukraine war and trade contestation between the world’s two largest economies were not achieved. Further 
amplifying uncertainty was the conflict and crisis that ensued in the Middle East impacting a region that constitutes 30% of 
global oil production. Global trade growth at 0.2% was the weakest performance outside of global recession in 50 years.
The the market in which we operate continued to experience the impact of global reality occasioned by, marked interest rate 
hikes by regulators, currency depreciation and inflation coupled with increased concerns on debt sustainability.
Our performance 
This challenging macro context has inevitably affected our stakeholders, particularly customers, who have had to bear 
the brunt of multiple impacts on their businesses and livelihoods. In response, the Group consciously chose to cushion its 
customers by moderating the impact of inflation into its operational costs and absorbing the rise on interest rates without 
transferring the full effect to its customers. Our actions have enabled businesses to continue operations, thus safeguarding 
employment, incomes and livelihoods.
This approach to stakeholders is a distinctive aspect of Equity Group. From inception, we have sought to proactively support 
our customers through relevant, affordable and easily accessible services and products. We understand that behind every 
account or transaction is a unique individual or organisation with specific requirements and goals. Our unique approach 
became even more apparent during the recent pandemic. As businesses, economies, and lives were drastically affected, 
we took it upon ourselves to ensure that our support to customers remained steadfast. During such uncertain times, the 
approach we take can make a significant difference to our customers' lives. 
Despite cushioning customers, the Group recorded strong returns notwithstanding a slowdown in its Kenyan subsidiary. 
Diversification provided an important anchor for the Group performance as subsidiaries in the Democratic Republic of the 
Congo (DRC), Rwanda, Tanzania and Uganda increased their contribution to overall revenues alongside our investment and 
insurance offerings. At a broader level, we continued stakeholder engagements with partners and funders as we sought 
to catalyse interest and involvement in the Africa Recovery and Resilience Plan (ARRP) and signed up to the Taskforce on 
Nature-related Financial Disclosures (TNFD) as an early adopter. Our efforts at driving sustainable practices have not gone 
unnoticed as the Group CEO was appointed to co-chair the Sustainable Markets Initiative Africa Chapter by King Charles III. 
Our social engine Equity Group Foundation (EGF) continues to provide support on environmental and social needs with total 
funds raised at USD 649 million while supporting 23,875 university scholars, 517,247 MSMEs with training on entrepreneurship 
and impacting 3.8 million farmers among other beneficiaries. Our Equity Afia franchise has continued to grow and has now 
expanded into DRC where we are looking at establishing 30 clinics. In Kenya we are currently at 98 clinics with an average 
70,000 visits per month.
Board matters
Governance remains a high priority area responding to internal dynamics including the continued maturity and growth of 
the Group and external aspects such as legislation and regulations. We strengthened the subsidiary boards through the 
nomination of new board members providing essential skills and expertise. We have revamped our boards in order for us to 
align board skills with our strategy in ARRP.
A key highlight of the Board was the acquisition of Compagnie Générale de Banque (Cogebanque) in Rwanda following 
regulatory and corporate approvals that were completed in November 2023. The Group acquired 99.125% of the issued share 
capital of Cogebanque, which was the fifth largest bank in Rwanda by assets, operating through 28 branches. This strategic 
acquisition was in line with our geographic expansion strategy that includes identifying synergistic entities for acquisition. This 
acquisition and subsequent amalgamation of the business with that of Equity Group's existing banking subsidiary in Rwanda 
on 31 December 2023, positioned Equity Bank as the 2nd largest bank in Rwanda after the merger.
CHAIRMAN’S STATEMENT

24
In 2023, we bade farewell to Evelyn Rutagwenda, after  she concluded a highly impactful nine-year tenure marked by integrity, 
professionalism and unwavering dedication to the Group. Her commitment to the ethos and purpose of our organisation has 
been exemplary, evident in the grace and wisdom she consistently brought to every board engagement. We recognise and 
celebrate her outstanding legacy with the Group and wish her all the best in her future endeavours confident that her impact 
will continue to be experienced in the coming years.
Looking forward
In the years ahead, the Board of Directors at Equity Group will devote their attention primarily to overseeing the implementation 
of the Africa Recovery and Resilience Plan (ARRP). The ARRP is a strategic initiative designed by us to drive the socio-economic 
transformation of Africa, particularly in the wake of a global pandemic that has underscored the need for resilience and 
recovery.
The primary focus of ARRP is complemented by traditional areas of board oversight on key facets of our operations such as 
risk management, regulatory compliance, performance assessments, and reward systems and will continue to be critical 
considerations. Likewise, emerging areas of importance like sustainability practices, and information technology require 
the Board's constant vigilance and control. Each of these areas presents its own unique challenges and opportunities, which 
necessitate thorough and continuous analysis, sound judgement and purposeful action.
Sustainability and IT, two areas that have taken on increased significance in recent years, will continue to be major areas 
of interest for the Board. Sustainability is not an isolated concern but integrates with all aspects of our operations and is 
central to our twin-engine model. The sustainability focus will be on developing and implementing strategies to reduce our 
environmental footprint, conserve resources, and promote business resilience.
Taken together, these traditional and emerging areas of focus reflect the range and complexity of responsibilities that the 
Board will embrace. As we continue this journey, we believe that resilient, effective, and responsive governance will enable us 
to achieve our strategic goals and generate long-term value for all our stakeholders.
Acknowledgements
The Board is continuously impressed by the passionate engagement and commitment shown by the Group's leadership and 
employees. The leadership has demonstrated consistency and courage while steering the Group, never avoiding difficult 
decisions and always available to support their teams. They are the torchbearers of our mission, setting the tone for our 
organisational culture and laying down the blueprint for our future growth through strategic foresight and sound judgement.
Our employees, the backbone of our operations, are equally noteworthy. Every single day, they bring in their talent, skills, and 
intellectual capital, fuelling our progress and growth. Their can-do spirit, readiness to embrace change, and their resilience 
in the face of adversity speak volumes about the strength of our organisational character.
Our customers form the lifeblood of our organisation. They are at the heart of everything we do, from strategy formulation to 
product development and service delivery. We also recognise our other stakeholders including investors, strategic partners, 
regulatory bodies, and the larger communities within which we operate. Their roles, influences, and interactions fundamentally 
shape our organisation's direction, making them intrinsic to our operations, strategic decisions, and success. 
The Board views this display of collaboration not merely as an asset but as a vital force imbued within the Group's DNA. It is 
what gives us confidence in our ability to deliver on our promises, navigate uncertainties, and builds the foundation upon which 
our future success will be built.

These global headwinds have cascaded across the regions where we operate with divergent outcomes mainly inflationary 
pressures, currency depreciation and interest rate hikes with marked impact on our customers. This has required us to 
take hard decisions on how to support our customers ensuring they weather these challenges and continue to operate, 
safeguarding incomes, jobs and livelihood. 
Yet despite the tough choices we have had to make to cushion customers from the full effect of interest rate hikes and bear 
the inflationary pressures in our operational costs, the Group has returned an improved performance compared to the prior 
year. What gives us pride is that we have built a culture that is responsive and adaptive to stakeholders underpinned by regular 
interaction and engagement. This is how we give life to our corporate purpose, values and philosophies and display their 
integration within our day-to-day operations.
Further, the Group continues to attract external accolades with Brand Finance Banking 500 ranking the Group as the second 
strongest banking brand in the world with an impressive Brand Strength Index (BSI) of 92.5 and an elite AAA+ brand strength 
rating. Additionally, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) rated the Group as leading globally in the number of loans 
issued on climate finance out of 149 banks assessed.
Our performance
The Group continued to perform robustly within a highly complex and challenging context. Revenue growth of 25% was 
recorded in the year increasing from Shs 145.9 billion to Shs 181.7 billion with 52% of this revenue being attributed to Kenya. 
Non-funded income saw a sharp rise by 28%, from Shs 59.9 billion in 2022 to Shs 76.9 billion buoyed by strong performance 
in the insurance, investment banking and trade finance offerings and contributing 42% of total income. Net interest income 
growth was muted due to the decision of the Group to cushion customers from the full effect of increased interest rates thus 
bearing an interest expense increase of 52% contrasted to an interest income increase of 30%. Consequently, net interest 
income saw a rise of 22%, from Shs 86 billion to Shs 104.8 billion.
Profit after Tax (PAT) stood at Shs 43.7 billion, a 5% decline compared to Shs 46.1 billion in 2022. This performance was 
strongly supported by growth in incomes for subsidiaries in DRC, Tanzania, and Rwanda as well as investment banking, 
and insurance. However, PAT decline was recorded for both the Kenya and Uganda subsidiaries, reflecting the challenging 
macro-environmental context. Overall, the Kenya subsidiary contribution to PAT was 55% with 45% coming from the other 
subsidiaries.
The Group's pursuit of geographical expansion and diversification continues to pay off. Customers across the regions continued 
to display their confidence in the Group leading to a customer deposit growth of 29% closing the year at Shs 1,358.2 billion. 
Loan growth at 26% was also achieved increasing the Loan Book to Shs 887.4 billion with Kenya constituting 51% of loans 
issued at Shs 448.7 billion. 
Non-performing loans, (NPLs) increased to 11.7% from 7.7% remaining below the industry average of 15%. To address the 
impact of this rise, the Group significantly increased its loan loss provisions by more than double to reach Shs 32.8 billion from 
Shs 13.7 billion. As a result, the Group has achieved a strong NPL coverage ratio at 67.3% based on provisions at an elevated 
cost of risk of 4.4% up from 2.4%.
Total costs grew by 52% as the Group opted to absorb the impact of global and regional inflation and depreciation of local 
currencies that saw staff expenses grow by 28% and other operating expenses by 39%. While the cost of funding and deposits 
rose by 53% and total operating costs grew by 52%, yields on loans only increased by 600 basis points from 12.1% to 12.7% as 
we focused on cushioning customers to enhance their chances of survival and resilience. 
Delivering on the ARRP
Our transformation plan, the Africa Recovery and Resilience Plan (ARRP) entered its second year in 2023. We have made 
marked progress in engaging with partners and funders to support the Plan receiving endorsements from leading African, 
global and United Nations agencies and governments. We have made good progress through the year in attaining the key 
objectives under the Plan as we increased our client numbers to 19.6 million customers up from 17.7 million. In addition, the 
number of borrowing businesses increased to 0.3 million while borrowing customers stood at 0.84 million. Overall, we have 
made good strides in pursuing the Plan. As the ARRP is strongly hinged on unlocking the primary sector in Africa, a major 
concern for the Group in the year revolved around nature and climate change.
In 2023, we signed up for the newly launched nature-focused standard, the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures 
(TNFD), as an early adopter, signalling our commitment to enhancing disclosures on nature and biodiversity. Further we

community’s efforts in addressing the risks associated with nature loss and exploring opportunities in Africa. 
Within the Group, we maintained momentum on delivering our sustainability strategy including the adoption and roll out of the 
Group’s ESG and Climate Risk Framework across all subsidiaries. A standalone sustainability management committee was 
established in the first quarter of the year and the Group’s Environmental and Social Risk Management policies were reviewed 
and updated. The Group continues to equip departments and subsidiaries’ ESG functions with adequate and skilled resources.
Social impact
The Equity Group Foundation (EGF) has made great strides in its operations across the region. Through the Shared Prosperity 
Model, EGF provides access to financial education, with a particular focus on women and youth. Through this program, 2,450,455 
women and youth have received financial education. Additionally, 517,247 micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) 
attended financial training to strengthen their entrepreneurial skills. 290,713 MSMEs under the 'Young Africa Works’ program 
in collaboration with Mastercard Foundation have received Shs 275.3 billion in financing. In the Food and Agricultural sector, 
3.8 million small-scale farmers accessed capacity-building and financing to scale their farming ventures. These initiatives 
also reached 292,362 small and medium-sized agri-businesses.
Under the Education and Leadership programmes of the  foundation, the  flagship 'Wings to Fly' and 'Elimu Scholarship' programs 
collectively benefited 60,009 secondary school students who had received comprehensive secondary school scholarships by 
the end of 2023. Additionally, the Equity Leadership Program has cumulatively onboarded  23,825 university scholars into 
the program including 891 global university scholars and 3,471 full scholarships for technical and vocational education and 
training (TVET) programs. In the health  sector, Equity Afia, grew its network of franchised outpatient medical centres  from 
77 in 2022 to 98 healthcare facilities. The facilities have cumulatively attended to 2,143,344 patient visits as at the close of the 
year. Under the foundation’s initiatives in the Energy, Environment and Climate Change, we had planted 25.2 million trees 
cumulatively by year end.
Looking Forward
Sustainability offers a viable path for global advancement, presenting an opportunity to establish economic, market, and social 
models that prioritise and reward sustainable practices. This is particularly crucial for Africa, a continent endowed with a vast 
wealth of natural resources. These resources, if managed efficiently and sustainably, can provide substantial solutions to a 
wide array of socio-economic issues, that plague the continent. However, the pressing necessity for swift and effective action 
to address barriers to financial and non-financial interventions for nature and climate is becoming increasingly paramount. 
We view our role as a catalyst of the transformation of the continent as critical for ensuring a sustainable future. By mobilising 
the agency of citizens and a cross section of stakeholders, we are committed to driving marked attention and effort to delivering 
for people and the planet. We are faced with a historical tipping point that requires urgency in delivering on the sustainable 
development goals (SDGs) that requires concerted and collective effort. This underscores our eagerness to engage in 
partnerships as we appreciate the scale and complexity of the global sustainability and climate challenge.

times, and to the executive team for the  exemplary leadership which has allowed us to attain high-quality outcomes. 
Our customers have demonstrated faith and fidelity to our brand while proving resilient and innovative. Our staff remain our 
key advocates and the champions of our purpose, tirelessly delivering value for stakeholders while holding true to the Group’s 
ethos and strategic intent. 
I am also grateful to our partners, funders, regulators, employees and policymakers for their unwavering support, counsel 
and goodwill, which has been vital in delivering for stakeholders.

Our material issues
In 2023, the global economy continued to recover and adjust from the shocks created by the COVID-19 pandemic, albeit slowly. 
Global growth was estimated at 3.1% with economies grappling with the pandemic’s aftermath, while concurrently facing new 
challenges such as geo-political tensions in Ukraine and the Middle East, effects of monetary tightening, increased impacts 
of climate variability, weak economic performance and trade tensions between major economies. On the positive side, the 
pandemic-forged era of digital transformation continued to thrive with a revamped digital economy increasing opportunities 
in e-commerce, remote work, and digital payment systems. These opportunities are however measured against having to 
address new challenges in areas of cybersecurity and digital taxation.
The continued pressures created by inflationary forces nudged regulators to continue with monetary interventions. The US 
Federal Reserve commenced interest rate hikes in March 2022, the first rate increase since 2018. By the close of 2023, and 
after to ten hikes, the rate closed at 5.25 – 5.50%. Regulators in the countries we operate in maintained a similar trend of rate 
hikes to contain inflation, safeguard livelihoods and protect their economies from recession.
Climate change featured prominently in the global dialogue underpinned by increased severity and frequency of climate 
disasters. Consideration of the green economy is gradually becoming a key driver of economic growth, with renewable energy, 
sustainable agriculture, and green technology taking centre stage. Financial institutions and businesses are increasingly 
incorporating environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors into their investing and operational considerations, 
signifying a major shift in global economic paradigms.
In the year, international trade continued to be reshaped following a rethink of global supply chains created by constraints 
due to production concentration in specific countries and regions. Countries are leaning towards regionalisation and near-
shoring, in a bid to build resilient and diversify supply chains. The shift from globalisation to 'slowbalisation' represents a 
fundamental restructuring of the global economy.
Global economic growth is projected to be 3.2% in 2024 and 2025, according to the International Monetary Fund with growth 
in leading economies expected to improve with most economic uplift coming from several large emerging markets and 
developing economies.

The Equity Group strategy is a multi-pronged and holistic solution to achieve the social and economic transformation of Africa. 
This unconventional strategy represents our belief that financial services are a critical facilitator of improving livelihoods, 
safeguarding nature and the environment and enabling social-economic development. The Plan focuses on three key 
approaches and is anchored on six key pillars, with a clear set of targets to be achieved by 2030.

on the enabling role of technology, trade and investment and achieving social and environmental impact.

MATERIAL MATTERS
A matter is considered material if it can substantively affect our ability to create value in the short, medium and long term. Our 
materiality process identifies our key material matters and the collective themes under which they fall. We apply integrated 
thinking to identify these matters which in turn informs our strategy as well as our approach to managing risk and maximising 
opportunities.
We use a three-step materiality process to determine matters that affect our ability to create value:
Identify
Prioritise
Integrate
In the identification phase, we evaluate significant 
issues in our operating environment that may 
impact our ability to create value and deliver 
our strategy. These issues could be financial, 
operational, reputational, environmental, social, 
strategic, or legislative. Our evaluation considers 
three key aspects:
How these issues affect the accessibility, 
availability, and affordability of our capitals. 
Legitimate stakeholder feedback.
Recent events as well as potential issues that 
could have a short, medium, or long-term impact 
on the Group.
Using the outcomes of this 
assessment, we prioritise 
matters that are most 
important to our ability to 
generate sustained value over 
time while considering key risks 
and opportunities.
We incorporate an approach 
to managing these identified 
material matters into our

GROUP ENTERPRISE RISK MANAGEMENT FRAMEWORK 
The Group’s Enterprise Risk Management Framework (Group ERMF), which is approved by the Board, supports achievement 
of strategic objectives by promoting foresight and risk-informed decision-making. It upholds a sound risk culture and 
outlines the key principles and practices for management of material risks, both financial and non-financial. It also promotes 
a consistent approach to identify, assess, manage and report the risks accepted and incurred, with clear accountabilities, 
and continuous monitoring of the risk environment. We continue to enhance our capabilities to ensure risk management is 
systematic, structured, and timely.
Risk culture 
The Group is committed to building and maintaining a sound risk culture. The Board is responsible for setting the right tone 
from the top to foster adequate risk awareness at all levels of the Group when engaging in strategic and operational decisions. 
Senior management is responsible for communicating and role modelling the expected values and norms in relation to risk-
taking and risk management to ensure a culture of integrity and high ethical standards, including formalising lessons learnt 
to prevent repetition of unwanted incidents and outcomes. 
Three lines of defense
The Group’s risk management approach follows the three-lines-of-defence model. The first line of defence are the functions 
which expose the Group to risk either through entering revenue generating or other transactions, or providing the operational 
support for such activities. The first line of defense owns and manages the risks arising in its activities. The second line of 
defence refers to the independent control functions led by the Group Chief Risk Officer that provide oversight and challenge 
of first line risk management processes and decisions to provide confidence to the Board. The third line of defense comprises 
the Group Internal Audit function led by the Group Chief Internal Audit Officer which provides to the Board independent 
assurance on the effectiveness of risk management controls implemented by the first and second lines of defense.
Principal Risk Types
The Group ERMF identifies and prioritises principal risks which individually or in combination can have material adverse 
impact on the financial performance or reputation of the Group. Prioritisation is based on the probability of occurrence and the 
consequences or impact should the event happen. They are managed through distinct Principal Risk Type Frameworks (PRT 
Frameworks) that set out the overall risk management approach for respective PRTs. 
The principal risks cover financial risk types (i.e. Credit Risk, Capital Risk, Liquidity Risk, Market Risk, Country Risk, Insurance 
Risk) and non-financial risk types (i.e. Strategic Risk, ESG/Climate Risk, Operational Risk, Reputational Risk, Compliance 
Risk, Financial Crime Risk, Conduct Risk, Fraud Risk, Model Risk and Technology, Information & Cybersecurity Risk). 
The Group continuously monitors its internal and external environment to identify and manage any emerging risks that could 
materially impact on its strategic objectives and that may require to be included in the ERMF. The Group ERMF and PRT 
Frameworks and the supporting policies and procedures are reviewed annually or more frequently if necessitated by material 
changes in the internal and/or external environment. 
The Group appoints Risk Framework Owners, Policy Owners, and Process Owners, in addition to the Group Chief Risk Officer, 
to ensure effective implementation of the Group ERMF, the PRT Frameworks, Policies and Procedures.
Risk governance 
The Board has ultimate responsibility for risk management and is supported by the Group Board Risk Committee. The 
management-level Group Non-Financial Risks Committee (GNFRC) and the Group Assets and Liabilities Committee are 
approved by the Board to provide proactive support to the Board by scrutinizing the management of key risks and the operation 
of internal controls.
The Board receives key information for the principal risk types covering the risk profile in the current and prior quarters, key 
internal and/or external risk drivers, and where appropriate the risk responses and timelines to control risk exposures within 
the board approved risk appetite level. The reports also include emerging risks and the associated responses.

Risk Appetite
The Board’s risk appetite statements articulate the aggregate level and types of risk that the Group is willing to accept to 
achieve its business objectives. The risk appetite statements cover all principal risk types both financial and non-financial. 
Various quantitative and qualitative metrics are monitored and reported to the Board to ensure adherence to the risk appetite 
statements.
OVERVIEW OF SELECT PRINCIPAL RISK TYPES
Credit risk 
The Group’s credit portfolio was resilient throughout 2023 as evidenced by stage 1 performing assets which comprised 78% of 
the total credit portfolio as at 31 December 2023 compared to 85% as at prior year end. This was despite significant headwinds 
including the residual Covid-19 effects, elevated inflation, rising interest rates, foreign exchange shortages and local 
currency depreciation. The development had been expected since Q4 2022, and changes made to strengthen the process for 
identification and closer management of vulnerable customers and segments. Provisions coverage remains satisfactory due 
to the increase in specific provisions given higher non-performing loans. The portfolio is well diversified across geographies, 
customer segments, industry sectors and products. 
Liquidity risk 
The Group continues to enjoy substantial core deposits which are generally stable, diversified and lower cost in nature. The 
main factors behind the stability of deposits include the large number of customers and extensive network of branches, agents 
and ATMs which are conveniently located across the six countries of operation, and the easily accessible digital channels. 
Furthermore, the Group maintains substantial liquidity reserves split between cash and government bonds, the latter being 
eligible for funding in the repo market in case of temporary need. 
Market risk  
The Group remained resilient despite the significant volatility in interest rates and regional currencies during 2023. Fair value 
gains and losses on the Group’s holdings of government securities under “Available For Sale” portfolio are recognised in the 
financial statements under “Other Comprehensive Income”.
Current indications point to a peaking of interest rates in major developed and developing markets with expectations of rate 
cuts later in the year. Furthermore, the Kenya Shilling has appreciated sharply against the US Dollar following sale by the 
Kenya Government of a USD 1.5 billion Eurobond which was highly oversubscribed and the proceeds utilised to buy back a 
large portion of the USD 2 billion Eurobond maturing in June 2024. 
Capital risk 
Capital risk is the risk of insufficient capital in relation to the amount required to carry out the Group’s strategy while satisfying 
regulatory capital adequacy requirements. The Group manages its business to avoid excessive losses and maintain a strong 
capital position including adequate management buffers under both normal and stressed economic conditions. Prudent 
capital risk management ensures adequate capital to support the Group’s growth ambitions and absorb unexpected losses 
without breaching regulatory capital requirements. The Group’s capital management practices include the Internal Capital 
Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP), internal capital targets, dividend distribution targets, stress testing, capital allocation, 
monitoring, and reporting. 
Financial crime risk 
Kenya was grey listed by the Financial Action Task Force in February 2024 following a review during 2023. Kenya joined other 
footprint markets on the grey list including the Demographic Republic of Congo, Tanzania, and South Sudan. The Group is 
implementing additional measures to further strengthen its capabilities in the prevention of financial crimes across all of the 
operating entities including enhancing human resources and systems, reviewing policies and procedures, scaling up general 
awareness and targeted training, and increasing testing of controls.
RISK STATEMENT

53
Compliance risk
The Group Compliance Risk Framework sets out the approach for identification and management of risks associated with 
all applicable laws and regulations. The Group has implemented processes to ensure compliance with applicable laws and 
regulations. The Group has no appetite for breaches in laws and regulations. Whilst regulatory noncompliance cannot be 
entirely avoided the Group strives to reduce this to an absolute minimum. 
Technology, information and cybersecurity risk
The Group’s continuing investments in infrastructure upgrades and digitalisation to increase capacity and enhance customer 
experience incurs technology, information, and cybersecurity risks. In line with the Group Technology, Information and 
Cybersecurity Risk Framework which sets out the approach for identification and management of these risks, the key focus 
areas during 2023 included: 
•	 Governance and oversight capabilities including people, processes and systems for risk management, management of 
information assets and third parties; and security awareness and training
•	 IT project management and software application development and management
•	 IT service management and resilience
•	 Access controls, data and infrastructure security and cybersecurity risk management 
Fraud risk
The Group Fraud Risk Management Framework sets out the approach to identification and management of fraud risks 
including controls and activities to prevent, detect and respond to frauds. 
Preventive controls and activities include:
•	 fraud risk assessments covering new and amended products and services, processes, channels, software applications and 
systems
•	 rigorous customer identity verification and strong customer authentication processes
•	 customer awareness campaigns 
•	 transaction limits and access controls
•	 employee screening and background checks
•	 employee fraud awareness training
•	 segregation of duties, and
•	 compliance with the Group Code of Conduct and other policies
Detective controls and activities include: 
•	 automated transaction monitoring
•	 reconciliations and reviews by the three lines of defence including Group Internal Audit, and 
•	 speak up and whistle blower hotlines and mechanisms.
Corrective and remedial actions include investigations, disciplinary actions, prosecutions, and recovery actions in respect of 
harm caused by frauds. 
The Group continues to enhance and adapt its capabilities including processes, systems and human resources and is leveraging 
on innovative technologies to cope with the evolving fraud typologies.

The Equity Group’s Human Resources Strategy has four strategic thrusts over the next two to three years:
1.	 Organising ourselves for growth through a market-focused target operating model and structure.
2.	 Delivering superior sustainable value creation for our stakeholders through a robust Productivity and Performance 
Management Framework.
3.	 Harnessing high employee engagement and retention through deployment of a competitive employee value proposition 
(including Total Rewards).
4.	 Building robust succession plans for key positions and career development pathways for our key talent.
In 2023 we continued to focus on sharpening our productivity and performance management approaches as we adopted the 
balanced score card to measure and review employee contributions. We now have productivity dashboards for Group as well 
as subsidiary teams. This is in line with our commitment to promote a high-performance culture that focuses on delivering 
value for stakeholders while ensuring the right employee experience.
We also focused our attention on building talent pools, succession planning and career development for our key talent. Learning 
for growth and inculcating a high-performance culture are key to our recipe for success. During the year, we requested all our 
employees to return to the office to align with our customers’ needs.
A top priority of the human capital function is to have the right organisation and the right talent to deliver on the commitments 
made under the Africa Recovery and Resilience Plan. This means organising employees to deliver and to be particularly 
market focused on how to create sustainable value for our stakeholders. We ensure that our employees have the right skill 
sets and right toolsets to deliver on their mandates. Back-office functions also need to enable and partner with the market 
facing teams to win in the marketplace. 
We continue to review and enhance our employee value proposition to ensure superior competitiveness and for talent retention 
as well as engagement.
Organisation design
In 2023 we finalised the re-design of our target operating model, built around 5 key broad categories of job families, namely: 
1)	 Demand – These teams develop and grow our customer base, target agreed to customer segments, and link these to 
specific sectors to customise relevant Customer Value Propositions.
2)	 Supply – These teams are responsible for demand fulfilment, designing and customising solutions, products and 
experience to specific customer segments and sectors.
3)	 Business Partners – These teams provide enabler subject matter expertise in the back-office centres of excellence to 
enable customer value creation along the organisations value chain. These include Strategy, Governance, Risk, and other 
technical subject-matter functions.
4)	 Subsidiaries/Licenses – These teams translate business strategy into customer value operationalisation through the 
regulated jurisdiction of operations across geographies. 
5)	 Shared Capabilities – These job families offer high volume, repetitive, standardized, and harmonised operational services, 
leveraging efficient, automated processes and policies to minimise duplication of resources and effort across geographies 
and licenses.

72
HUMAN CAPITAL
The above organisational design operates in a matrix reporting structure, whereby subsidiary teams report functionally into 
the Group Functional Leaders and operationally into the Subsidiary Executive Team. The Group Functional Leaders provide the 
subsidiary functional teams with strategic thought-leadership, functional risk oversight, build organisation-wide capacity and 
capabilities, enable best-practice sharing and ensure standardisation of policies, processes, and procedures. The Subsidiary 
Executive Teams manage the subsidiary functional teams to ensure the day-to-day execution and compliance with agreed 
periodic operating plans.
To further optimise our human resources, the HR teams in collaboration with business leaders at Group and in the 
subsidiaries conducted a comprehensive study of the Work, Workforce and Workplace to understand how our execution is 
aligned to our strategy. This was followed by Group CEO-led organisation-wide conversations; focus groups to facilitate an 
organisational health diagnostic assessment, including the unpacking of core capabilities such as: Governance, Leadership, 
Strategy, Structure, Systems and Processes, People, Products and how we create value for our customers. The outcomes of 
these engagements have led to the development of action plans which are strengthening our market leadership as we create 
sustainable stakeholder value.
Shared Prosperity Model
In line with the Shared Prosperity philosophy, in 2023, the Group recommended a fit-for-purpose Employee Share Ownership 
Plan (ESOP) for permanent employees of the Group and its subsidiary companies. The ESOP will result in employees being 
entitled to 198.6 million shares of the company. The ESOP seeks to align staff interests and aspirations with shareholders’ 
long-term goals, attracting and retaining talent, driving a performance culture, and giving a sense of ownership and shared 
purpose for employees.
Employee Wellness 
The Group views employee wellness through a holistic Wellness Wheel comprised of eight aspects including physical, 
intellectual, emotional, social, spiritual, financial, and environmental wellbeing. The wellness approach covers all these 
aspects striving to enable the protection and enhancement of employee wellbeing. The Group maintains an employee medical 
scheme managed through  Equity Afia medical facilities designated as the first point of call for outpatient medical services. 
The Group conducted employee outreach and experiential programs to create awareness on the different aspects of the 
scheme which included case management, life-threatening diseases, communicable disease management, occupational 
health and safety, as well as regular medical check-ups, among other interventions.
Diversity, Equality and Inclusion
The Justice, Equality, Diversity and Inclusion (JEDI) policy aims at creating an inclusive, equitable workplace where all 
employees can thrive and grow to realise their full potential.  The policy further provides guidance for the development and 
implementation of relevant plans, programs, and initiatives to recognise and promote workforce diversity and create a sense 
of belonging as they relate to the Group’s essence (Purpose, Vision, Mission and Values).
We are committed to supporting women employees to thrive and excel holistically including establishing forums for 
engagement. The Equity women EQUIP Book Club Cycle 3 featured a review of "The Psychology of Money" by Morgan Housel 
at the beginning of the year. This book review attracted 766 active members, forming 77 groups with approximately 10 
participants each across the Group.
The official launch of the Equity men’s club took place in February 2023. The club provides a forum for the male fraternity at 
Equity to share experiences while exploring opportunities for personal and professional growth. Dubbed, MANDATE, it aims 
to provide valuable insights into how men can navigate the world successfully and achieve excellence through networking, 
social interaction, and collaboration.
During the meeting, a book titled “The Leader Who Had No Title“, by Robin Sharma was presented to men ahead of the 
inauguration of the Equity Men's Book Club. The book club will provide a forum where members can participate by reading 
books and sharing learnings to support their growth in areas of career, family, and society.

Creating Value through technology
Information Technology (IT) facilitates and promotes the Group’s commercial and social engines. As technology changes 
rapidly, IT enables the business by building future-proof foundations. The strategic intent for IT is to build systems and 
processes that provide stability and reliability and adapt to future technological shifts. As Equity Group aims to acquire 100 
million customers by 2030, IT will play a critical role in delivering excellent digital technology solutions, providing innovative 
products and services to customers fostered by consistent, reliable, cost effective, scalable, and secure IT solutions. The IT 
department is designed to align with the ARRP as an enabling function and is a shared service across the organisation with 
specialists distributed across the product house, commercial and social aspects of the business.
Our IT Plan 2024: Building future proof foundations

with local and international development organisations, government, and the private sector. Based in Nairobi, Kenya, and with

Tax Sustainability 
Taxation and tax policies play a crucial role in the functioning of organisations, the society and governments across the globe. 
They are integral components of economic systems and have far-reaching implications for businesses, governments, and 
society as a whole.
As a leading financial institution, Equity Group recognises the crucial role it plays in this intricate tax framework and therefore, 
sustainability and ESG must always be at the top of its leadership agenda. 
Equity Group is also aware of the various tax measures that the governments have put in place for the collection of revenue, 
as a fuel for economic stability, promoting investment and building international competitiveness and trade relations. Equity 
Group has therefore taken a socially responsible approach to tax as a way of doing business. Our approach is therefore not 
only looking at tax compliance as the right thing to do but as a key driver to ensuring sustainable growth.
Our tax policy is a crucial element towards developing sustainability into our operations effectively. It serves as a cornerstone 
for ethical governance, financial transparency, and societal contribution. By establishing clear guidelines and principles 
regarding tax compliance, Equity Group not only upholds legal obligations but also fosters trust and credibility among 
stakeholders. Our tax policy, underpinned by robust controls demonstrates our commitment to ethical business practices, 
financial integrity, and the holistic well-being of society.
Our tax policy speaks to this through continuous self-reviews, taking advantage of voluntary disclosure programs offered 
by governments, continuous training of our teams to enable them to keep abreast with the ever-changing tax landscape, 
collaborative approaches with every stakeholder, including all Governments in the various jurisdictions in which we operate. 
It is this approach to tax transparency and accountability that the Group intends to use to build trust in its business for both 
internal and external stakeholders. 
In pursuing compliance, in the year ending 31st December 2023, Equity Group paid taxes amounting to Shs 29.7 billion 
comprising of direct taxes amounting of Shs 16.5 billion and indirect taxes of Shs 13.2 billion-accounted for and remitted 
through 864 tax returns throughout the year in the respective countries where we operate.
Scope and Approach
Today, we appreciate that tax is no longer about being compliant but also has far reaching effects on the sustainability of 
our organisation, governments and at the very essence- society.  The obligations that we have to society as a business that 
must comply with its tax obligations and a conduit that also facilitates revenue collection for the various governments applies 
consistently in our business dealings.
As a Group that presents itself as a sustainable business, we approach tax not only from the legal and economic perspective 
but also from an ethical perspective. In line with our Group Tax Policy and the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Standards for Tax 
(GRI -207), Equity Group applies the following approach and initiatives to promote and ensure tax transparency, accountability, 
and sustainability across the Group:
•	 Compliance: we are committed to 100% compliance with all relevant tax laws, regulations, and reporting requirements 
in the jurisdictions where we operate. This is by meeting our tax obligations through ensuring transparent and ethical 
practices, continuous engagement with stakeholders and direct engagement with government agencies, to facilitate and 
ensure compliance with all applicable tax laws, rules, and regulations in the respective jurisdictions where we operate. 
•	 Transparency: we appreciate that there is more to tax than just compliance. Embracing a culture of transparency and 
accountability in tax matters not only supports the Group’s long-term financial health but also reinforces its commitment 
to ethical business practices and social responsibility. This is intended to enable the public and the authorities to evaluate 
our business. For this reason, the Group openly discloses relevant information about its tax practices, policies, and 
contributions to tax authorities, stakeholders, and the public. We have in place a robust transfer pricing document and 
policy and continue to adhere to the country-by-country reporting regulations in place. Through this report, we disclose our

CORPORATE GOVERNANCE STATEMENT
Our governance structures
“Our corporate governance is integral to the Group’s financial, human, intellectual, social, and relational assets, exerting 
influence across all facets of our structure and operations. The Board acknowledges the pivotal role of robust corporate 
governance principles as the bedrock upon which stakeholder trust is established. Board members are deeply committed 
to upholding their responsibility towards the corporate governance agenda of the Group, demonstrating a steadfast 
dedication to sustaining the highest standards of corporate governance and ethical business practices. This commitment is 
driven by the aim to fulfil the needs and objectives of diverse stakeholders, fostering value creation throughout the Group’s 
operations.”
The Group is diverse and as such has established a comprehensive Corporate Governance Framework which sets out a 
schedule of matters with the objective of ensuring effective governance across the Group and furthering the value of the 
common brand.
During the year under review, the Group complied with all the aspects of the 2015 Capital Markets Authority (CMA) Code of 
Corporate Governance as highlighted under the following broad topics: 
•	 Board operations and control 
•	 Rights of shareholders 
•	 Stakeholder relations 
•	 Ethics and social responsibility 
•	 Accountability, risk management and internal control 
•	 Transparency and disclosure. 
The CMA Code of Corporate Governance has been made available to directors and senior management by uploading on the 
Group’s Board portal (eBoard). 
Board operations and control
The Group adheres strictly to the varied principles set out in the CMA Code of Corporate Governance with regard to Board 
operations and control: 
Appointment, composition, number and qualifications of Board members
Appointments to each of the Group boards is made in line with the Board Appointments Policy and Procedure through an 
organised and effective process that ensures the appointment of a diverse and balanced mix of proficient individuals. Such 
appointments consider academic qualifications, technical expertise, experience, nationality, age, gender, integrity and ethical 
standards. 
Recommendations for new nominees for appointment to the Board are made by the Group Board Governance, Nominations 
and Compensation Committee. In order to make it effective, the Board’s size, diversity and demographics are taken into 
consideration when electing Board members. The Group has a comprehensive Board Diversity Policy and Skills Matrix in 
place.
Diversity applies to academic qualifications, technical expertise, relevant banking knowledge, experience, nationality, age and 
gender so as to ensure a balanced Board that fairly reflects the Group’s shareholders and other stakeholders and provides a 
mechanism for the representation of minority shareholders. 
The Board as currently constituted, reflects broad diversity through variation in directors’ age, gender, professional 
qualifications, experience as well as nationality. The majority of the directors are members of professional bodies. A Board 
Succession Policy and Plan is also in place to ensure the smooth transition of Board members. 
Structure of the Group Board
Based on the current Articles of Association, the Board is required to comprise a minimum of seven directors, with the 
maximum set at 12. Various Board committees have been established with defined terms of reference to advise on key Group

93
CORPORATE GOVERNANCE STATEMENT
functions, including audit, finance, strategy, investment, IT and innovation, risk management, sustainability, governance and 
remuneration. The Board ensures these committees have suitable compositions, with members possessing the requisite 
skills for fulfilling their respective mandates.
Functions of the Board
In guiding the Company strategically and overseeing it with accountability to shareholders, the Board acts in the best interest 
of the Group and stakeholders, cognisant of its fiduciary duties in fulfilling its role and responsibilities. The Board has thus 
ensured that: 
•	 Roles reserved for the Board and those delegated to management are clearly distinguished. 
•	 The functions of the Chairperson and the CEO are exercised by separate individuals. 
•	 The Chairperson of the Board is an independent non-executive director. 
•	 There are established procedures to allow directors access to relevant, accurate and complete information and professional 
advice in order to discharge their duties effectively. 
•	 The Group’s strategy promotes sustainability. 
•	 There exist policies on related-party transactions and conflict of interest. 
•	 The Board is assisted by a suitably qualified and competent Company Secretary and 
•	 IT-related matters and innovation are exhaustively deliberated and addressed.
Board independence
The Board has clearly distinguished between its independent and non-independent members. To ensure independence, the 
tenure of an independent Board member may not exceed a cumulative term of six years. However, where an independent 
Board member attains a cumulative term of nine years, that member may continue to serve on the Board subject to re-
designation as a non-independent member. The Board assesses the independence of its members on an annual basis to 
mitigate the risks arising from potential conflicts of interest or undue influence from interested parties. 
Age limit for Board members
The age limit for directors has been set at 70 years. Any director who attains the age of 70 years will resign from the office 
of director at the following Annual General Meeting (AGM), and shareholders are informed of the resignation at each AGM. If 
any such director wishes to continue serving in the office of director, he/she must seek the approval of the shareholders at 
the AGM. 
Board tools
The Board employs tools for effective mandate fulfillment. Ethical standards are formalised in the Code of Conduct and Ethics, 
and the Board Charter outlines key values, principles, and operation mode. An annual Work Plan guides activities including 
a Board evaluation. To enhance effectiveness, an online paperless platform, eBoard, is used for performance assessment by 
an independent third-party consultant. The Board Charter and Code of Conduct and Ethics have been published in the Group’s 
website. 
Insider dealings/trading
As a publicly listed entity, and in strict adherence to its continuing listing obligations, the Group prohibits insider trading in 
order to restrict anyone who has access to non-public information from potentially profiteering or avoiding loss unfairly. In 
this regard, the Group has in place an insider-trading and market-abuse policy which has been made available to all staff to 
ensure compliance. 
Board induction, continuous skills   development, and training
The Group is dedicated to promptly inducting newly appointed Board members and ensuring their access to ongoing 
development programs, including business-awareness sessions. This commitment aims to empower members in maintaining, 
deepening, and updating their knowledge and skills for effective Board responsibilities. The Group has a well-defined Board 
Induction and Development Policy, evident in the various induction sessions of new directors. This comprehensive approach 
aligns with the Group’s commitment to continuous improvement and excellence in corporate governance, fostering a dynamic

and informed Board to meet evolving challenges and opportunities in their roles. The Group recognises that no matter how 
diligently candidates have been prepared for Board roles, nothing replaces formal orientation for new Board members.  The 
Group is therefore committed to ensuring that its Board members are inducted into their role as soon as they are appointed, 
and that they remain up-skilled and capable of delivering on their role and responsibilities. 
Training
Board members are provided with regular updates on matters relevant to legal reforms, corporate governance, the corporate 
environment, regulatory obligations, business and commercial risks and other matters that may be of interest in the execution 
of their role. 
In addition to the Leadership and Immersion Programme, the training programmes provided to directors in the year 2023 
included: 
•	 Compliance (Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Combating of Terrorism Financing (7 hours)
•	 Information Technology (IT) and Cybersecurity Governance (7 hours)
•	 Finance and Audit (4 hours)
•	 Environmental and Social Governance (4 hours)
Annual Board evaluation
The Board undertakes an annual assessment of its own performance, the performance of its chairperson, that of its committees, 
individual members, the Group CEO and Managing Director (MD), Group Executive Director and the Company Secretary. 
Following the evaluation exercise, which is led by an independent consultant, the Board deliberates on the evaluation results 
and subsequently implements their recommendations. 
The 2023 Board evaluation was duly conducted during the year under review, and the results noted for action. As required by 
the regulations within their respective jurisdiction of operation, the reports were filed with the regulators. 
Division of role of Chairperson and Chief Executive Officer
The Chairperson 
The Board is led by an Independent Non-Executive Chairperson to bolster its independent oversight. The role of the Chairperson 
is to: 
•	 provide leadership to the Board; 
•	 ensure that effective corporate governance practices and processes are embedded within the Group; and 
•	 ensure that the Board is functioning as required and playing its role effectively. 
In order to provide effective oversight, the Chairperson is not involved in the day-to-day running of the Group and acts as the 
liaison between the Board and executive management. 
The Chairperson also ensures that there is effective engagement between the Group and its stakeholders. 
The Chief Executive Officer 
•	 The Group Chief Executive Officer (GCEO) is a member of the Board and is responsible for: 
•	 the operations and management of day-to-day affairs of the Group: 
•	 ensuring that the Group remains purpose-driven and achieves the strategic objectives set by the Board; 
•	 providing leadership to senior management and staff; 
•	 overseeing the implementation of the decisions of the Board; 
•	 ensuring the preparation of strategy, annual budgets and business plans for approval by the Board; 
•	 establishing appropriate risk-management frameworks and internal controls; and 
•	 ensuring that the Group’s operations are consistent with its risk appetite.

•	 implementing a system of employment that is fair, safe, challenging and rewarding; 
•	 building a culture of trust, team spirit, integrity, collaboration, excellence and accountability; and 
•	 implementing appropriate processes for staff succession planning.
Rights of shareholders
The Group is steadfast in its commitment to safeguarding the legitimate interests of all shareholders while maintaining 
accountability to them. Shareholders possess the right to receive crucial information affecting their shareholding, participate 
in shareholder meetings, and engage in resolutions pertinent to their interests. Beyond basic voting rights, shareholders play 
a pivotal role in approving major strategic and corporate decisions with substantial impacts. An investor relations docket, led 
by the Group Chief Strategy Officer, ensures continuous engagement. Regular activities, including quarterly investor briefings 
and individual shareholder meetings/calls upon request, underscore the Group’s dedication to transparent communication 
and responsiveness. Our shareholders generally enjoy the right to: 
•	 Participate and vote in shareholder meetings. 
•	 Inspect corporate documents. 
•	 Elect directors. 
•	 Be sufficiently informed. 
•	 Registration of ownership. 
Information on the Group’s performance and other material public information is made available through the distribution of 
integrated reports and investor briefings, as well as on the Company’s website. 
For more on our shareholders, see page 105 and 106.
Stakeholder relations
The Board acknowledges the Group’s accountability to diverse stakeholders such as shareholders, employees, customers/
depositors, suppliers, development partners, financiers, governments, regulators, and local communities. Emphasizing the 
highest standards of conduct aligned with core values, the Group fosters effective relationships with stakeholders. Committed 
to building mutually beneficial ties, the Group strives to maintain a balance between individual stakeholder interests and those 
of the overall Group, promoting harmony and sustainability in its operations. In particular, the Group: 
•	 promotes fair, just and equitable employment policies; 
•	 promotes and is sensitive to the preservation and protection of the natural environment; 
•	 is sensitive to and conscious of gender interests and concerns; 
•	 promotes and protects the rights of children and other vulnerable groups; 
•	 enhances and promotes the rights and participation of host communities; and 
•	 supports staff and customer sensitisation. 
The Group encourages feedback from all stakeholders via various channels including but not limited to general meetings, 
investor briefings, customer surveys, whistleblowing and feedback forms. This feedback in turn informs the Board on the 
issues that stakeholders are most concerned with, and these are considered when formulating the Group’s strategy. 
For more on our stakeholders, see page 50. 
Compliance with laws and regulations
As a licensee of the CBK and listed on the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE) and cross-listed on the Uganda Securities 
Exchange (USE) and the Rwanda Stock Exchange (RSE), the Group is bound by and complies with: 
•	 the Banking Act and all prudential guidelines and directions given by the CBK and other regional regulators; 
•	 the Companies Act CAP 486, its regulations and amendments; 
•	 the Capital Markets Act and all subsidiary legislation;

Group is listed, together with any requirements, decisions, or directions given by these authorities and the exchanges; and

Transparency and disclosure
We have consistently practiced balanced disclosure of all material information concerning the Group.  We publish on our 
website important company information including, but not limited to, financial statements, investor briefings, particulars of 
shareholding, Group Notices and AGM material, our Group Board Charter, our Group Corporate Governance Framework, code 
of ethics and key Group policies including the Group Transparency and Disclosure Policy. 
Ethics and social responsibility
We believe that corporate governance is not just about ensuring that the Group complies with applicable laws, regulations, 
codes and the highest standards of corporate governance, but that it does so in a transparent and ethical manner. We are 
cognisant of the fact that it is in the interest of the Group to operate within the mandate entrusted to it by society, and to remain 
socially responsible. For this reason, we undertake our business in a manner that does not harm, and is respectful to, our 
beneficiaries and our customers. 
A Code of Ethics and Conduct has been developed and disclosed on our website. The Code of Ethics has also been cascaded 
to all directors and employees, noting that it is to be strictly adhered to, so as to ensure that the highest ethical standards 
are achieved. To foster compliance with the code, it is factored into the performance evaluation, weighted with respect to the 
significance of our values as a measure in the overall scorecard of each employee.

The Group remains a leading player, through the Equity Group Foundation, in innovative social payment solutions that offer

on energy, environment, and climate change, such as the Kenya off-grid solar access programme, the water harvesting and 
storage project, and clean energy for learning institutions and tree-planting, add both social and business value. 
For more on the EGF and our social impact strategies and programmes, see page 80 to page 87.
Policy on conflict of interest
The Board has established a Conflict-of-Interest Policy to offer guidance on how to mitigate the risk of activities and access 
to information that may lead to actual or potential conflicts of interest between the interests of the Group and those of its 
relevant persons. 
This is in recognition of the fact that it is not possible to foresee every situation that could give rise to real, apparent or 
potential conflicts of interest. The policy identifies the activities which may compete or conflict with the Group’s interests and 
outlines the steps to manage any conflicts of interest, should they arise. 
Whistleblowing policy
The purpose of the Whistleblowing Policy is to foster an environment and culture of information sharing, both positive and 
negative, without fear of retaliation. The policy and procedure manual is designed to enable stakeholders to speak up on, 
among others, their experiences, observations and opinions on products, service delivery, expectations, and challenges. It 
also encourages employees and other relevant stakeholders to report any perceived act of impropriety based on knowledge 
of facts. 
Policy on procurement
The Board has developed a Group Procurement Policy, in order to: 
•	 promote best practices, transparency and professionalism in all acquisition processes within the Group; 
•	 ensure that suppliers of goods and services are subjected to a competitive tendering process in order to achieve quality, 
price competitiveness and reliability;

•	 ensure that all expenditure is in accordance with prior approved budget and procurement plans; and 
•	 ensure compliance with applicable regulations and legislations. 
Accountability, risk management and internal control
In order to help manage risks we have developed a risk- intelligent culture that is founded on: 
•	 The Group’s core values 
•	 Risk-based incentives 
•	 Group risk governance structure 
•	 Risk-management tools and framework 
•	 Accountability 
In the context of the prevailing regulatory and economic environment, we assume various kinds of risks in our business, 
and we support activities in pursuit of the attainment of our strategic objectives. We recognise that sound risk management 
contributes to the Group’s long-term financial stability. 
The Group Integrated Risk Management Policy outlines our risk management framework, risk appetite- setting framework, 
risk evaluation and reporting, and harmonises risk policies across the Group. 
Assurance is guaranteed through the risk department, internal audit, compliance and enforcement teams, external audit, 
Central Bank inspection, CMA and NSE reviews and cross border supervisory colleges, as well as by credit rating agencies’ 
reviews. 
In addition, in line with the Equity 3.0 strategy, we continue to leverage technology and innovation to review risks through a 
holistic approach, and which is reported to our stakeholders. 
For more on risk management, see pages 51 - 53. 
Directors’ remuneration report
The Board reviews and recommends the remuneration structure of directors annually, subject to shareholders’ approval. 
While directors’ remuneration is linked to performance, it is competitively structured to attract and retain the best talent to 
effectively develop the Group’s business. Particulars of compensation of directors and key personnel are disclosed to the 
public in our audited financial statements in our remuneration report on pages 115-117. 
Executive directors
The Executive Directors’ remuneration package comprises core fixed elements (base salary, pension and other benefits). 
Executive directors are eligible to participate in the Group’s bonus scheme, which is anchored on the achievement of KPIs, but 
they are not entitled to earn fees or sitting allowances. 
Non-executive directors
Non-executive directors are appointed for a renewable term of three years, subject to requisite regulatory and shareholder 
approval. They are obligated to act reasonably, in good faith and in the best interests of the Group and its shareholders. Non-
executive directors are vested with the key responsibilities of: 
•	 constructively challenging and contributing to the development of strategy, and extending the business of the Group; 
•	 monitoring the performance of management in meeting agreed goals and objectives, and the reporting of performance; 
and 
•	 ensuring that financial information is accurate, and that financial controls and systems of risk management are robust, 
scalable and defensible.

Non-Executive Directors are entitled to sitting allowances for attending Board and committee meetings, as well as an out-of-
station per diem for attending to Group business outside their usual place of business or residence. Non-executive directors 
do not earn a salary and they do not participate in the Group’s bonus schemes or the Group’s pension plan. Upon retirement or 
termination, non-executive directors are entitled to any accrued but unpaid directors’ fees or reasonably incurred expenses, 
but not to any other compensation. 
Insurance
The Group provides Directors’ and Officers’ Liability Insurance for all directors during the entire duration of their tenure. 
Except in instances of negligence, the Group indemnifies its directors against all and any liabilities, losses and claims arising 
from their position as directors, including all legal and other professional expenses incurred in defending any civil or criminal 
action against themselves or the Group in connection with their bona fide conduct of its affairs. We have put in place a Directors 
and Officers Insurance Cover to cover the discharge of their obligations as directors.
